summary:
André Jobin (1786–1853) was a Montreal notary and French-Canadian political figure who supported the Patriote movement and later the LaFontaine–Baldwin reform alliance. He qualified as a notary in 1813 and built a large practice, serving clients from labourers to merchants and real-estate speculators. He also published a map of Montreal and the island in 1834.

A supporter of Louis-Joseph Papineau, Jobin entered the Lower Canada Assembly in 1835. He opposed the government’s response to the 1832 Montreal election riots and helped organise resistance to colonial policies. During the 1837–38 rebellion, he went into hiding, was arrested and charged with sedition, but was released without trial. The suspension of Lower Canada’s constitution ended his Assembly seat.

After the union of the Canadas, Jobin served in the Assembly from 1843 to 1851. He backed responsible government, the Rebellion Losses Bill and measures supporting French-language rights. He also secured reforms to the regulation of notaries. Later, he helped establish Montreal’s savings bank and served as the first president of the Montreal Board of Notaries.
